overview.title: From beetle prototypes to program-centric analogy
overview.section: 19.4 The missing ingredients: Search and symbols
overview.main_topic: Figure 19.12 (value-centric abstraction), the end of the value-centric discussion, and the introduction of program-centric analogy as exact structural matching (subgraph isomorphism)
overview.central_idea: Value-centric analogy is fast, approximate and intuitive. Program-centric analogy is slow, exact and deliberate: it relates things by whether parts of them have exactly the same structure (e.g., shared subgraphs in programs' operator graphs), and it underlies reasoning, planning and rigor.
overview.importance: This page introduces the second pole of abstraction, the one the book says deep learning is missing (p.612) and that program synthesis aims to provide (p.613).
learning_objectives: Read Figure 19.12 as the value-centric pipeline
Give everyday examples of value-centric abstraction (tasks done without thinking, typecasting movie characters)
Define program-centric analogy and contrast it with similarity comparison
Explain subgraph isomorphism in the context of refactoring code
Recognize program-centric analogies outside computer science (reasoning, planning, rigor)
prerequisites: Programs or computations as graphs of operators (computation graphs, p.71)
Basic software engineering: functions, classes, inheritance

summary:
**Figure 19.12** shows value-centric analogy in three panels: *Instances in the wild* (various beetles), *Similarity clustering* (the beetles grouped into two dashed circles of look-alikes), and *Abstract prototypes* (two dark silhouettes, one per cluster, matching no particular beetle).

The sentence from p.609 ends: value-centric abstraction underlies *pattern recognition, perception, and intuition*. If you can do a task **without thinking about it**, you rely heavily on value-centric analogies. Subconsciously sorting movie characters into "types" is value-centric abstraction.

**Program-centric analogy.** Cognition is more than this immediate, approximate, intuitive categorization. A second mechanism for generating abstractions is **slower, exact, deliberate**: program-centric (or structure-centric) analogy.

The example comes from software engineering. You notice that several functions or classes have a lot in common and ask whether a more abstract function could do the job and be reused, or whether an abstract base class could be shared through inheritance. You are *not* comparing them by *how similar* they look, the way you'd compare faces with an implicit distance function. You are asking whether **parts** of them have **exactly the same structure**. This is a search for a **subgraph isomorphism** (Figure 19.13, p.611): programs can be represented as **graphs of operators**, and you look for subgraphs (program subsets) shared exactly across programs.

This kind of analogy-making, exact structural match within discrete structures, is not limited to computer science or mathematics. People use it constantly without noticing. It underlies **reasoning**, **planning**, and the general idea of **rigor** (as opposed to intuition). Whenever you think about objects connected by a **discrete network of relationships** rather than a continuous similarity function, you are using program-centric analogies.

paragraphs.excerpt: recognition, perception, and intuition. If you can do a task without thinking
paragraphs.what_it_says: Finishing the sentence from p.609: value-centric abstraction underlies pattern recognition, perception and intuition. Tasks you do without thinking rely heavily on value-centric analogies, and subconsciously classifying movie characters into 'types' is an example.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Without thinking' is the diagnostic: value-centric processing is automatic and immediate, a single lookup against learned prototypes. Recognizing a face, reading a word or sensing that a character is 'the mentor type' happens in a flash, with no explicit steps. This is the same kind of computation as a forward pass of a trained network.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a self-test for which pole a task uses: if no deliberate steps are needed, it's mostly value-centric.

paragraphs.what_it_means: The two poles differ in speed and precision. Value-centric is fast and approximate, while program-centric is slow and exact. The pairing loosely resembles the familiar 'System 1 / System 2' distinction, though the book does not use those terms (note not in the book).

paragraphs.excerpt: In software engineering, you often write different functions or classes that seem
paragraphs.what_it_says: Programmers notice redundancies between functions or classes and ask whether a more abstract reusable function, or a shared abstract base class, could replace them. That definition of abstraction is program-centric analogy. You aren't comparing by how similar they look, as with faces and an implicit distance function. You're asking whether parts of them have exactly the same structure, which is a subgraph isomorphism (Figure 19.13): programs are graphs of operators, and you look for subgraphs shared exactly across programs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two pieces of code can look different (different variable names, different surrounding code) and still contain the *same computation*. The DRY principle and refactoring are this kind of analogy: you identify the identical structure, extract it as a function with parameters for what differs, and reuse it. 'Exactly' is the important word. A function that is 'almost' the same structure cannot be factored out without changing behavior, while two faces that are 'almost' alike are simply similar. The relation is all-or-nothing on structure, though it ignores surface details such as names.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Software engineering is something every reader of this book does, so it makes the abstract idea concrete. It also suggests that program synthesis (p.613) and library learning, which means finding reusable functions across programs, are the machine counterparts.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Subgraph isomorphism: given graphs G and H, find a subgraph of G that is structurally identical to H (a one-to-one mapping of nodes preserving edges and operator labels). Finding the largest subgraph shared by two programs is a discrete combinatorial search problem (the general subgraph-isomorphism problem is NP-complete; not stated in the book).

terminology.meaning: An exact structural match between part of one graph and another graph (or part of it).
A representation of a program where nodes are operations (+, =, loops, conditionals) and edges show data/control flow.
A class capturing structure shared by several subclasses, which inherit it.

paragraphs.excerpt: This kind of analogy-making via exact structural match within different discrete structures
paragraphs.what_it_says: Exact structural matching isn't limited to computer science or mathematics: people use it constantly without noticing. It underlies reasoning, planning and the general concept of rigor (as opposed to intuition). Whenever you think about objects connected by a discrete network of relationships, not a continuous similarity function, you're using program-centric analogies.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Examples beyond the book: recognizing that a family tree and a corporate org chart have the same 'reports to' structure; seeing that a new board-game situation is a fork you know from chess; planning a trip as a sequence of connected steps where each depends on the previous. What these share is *discrete relations* (connected or not, before or after), not degrees of resemblance.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that program-centric abstraction is a general cognitive capacity, which makes its absence from deep learning a central gap rather than a niche one.

concepts.name: Value-centric analogy / abstraction
concepts.definition: Abstraction formed by comparing instances with a continuous similarity function, clustering them, and merging clusters into prototypes.
concepts.intuition: Instant 'that's a beetle' or 'that's the villain type' recognition.
concepts.technical: Distance on a latent manifold; prototypes as cluster representatives; nearest-prototype categorization (p.609).
concepts.significance: It underlies pattern recognition, perception and intuition: tasks done without thinking.
concepts.misconception: That fast and intuitive means unreliable. It works well wherever the manifold hypothesis holds and data is plentiful.

concepts.name: Program-centric (structure-centric) analogy
concepts.definition: Abstraction formed by finding parts of different instances that have exactly the same structure and isolating them as a shared, reusable abstraction.
concepts.intuition: Spotting the same loop in two functions and turning it into one helper function.
concepts.technical: Instances are discrete structures (e.g., graphs of operators); relatedness is subgraph isomorphism; merging means extracting the shared subgraph as a new unit.
concepts.significance: It underlies reasoning, planning and rigor. The book argues deep learning lacks it (p.612).
concepts.example: Extracting compute_mean from two code fragments (Figure 19.13, p.611); introducing an abstract base class.
concepts.misconception: That it is only for programmers or mathematicians. The book says everyone uses it constantly without noticing.

concepts.name: Subgraph isomorphism
concepts.definition: An exact structure-preserving match between a subgraph of one graph and another graph.
concepts.intuition: Finding the same pattern of connections, regardless of how the nodes are named.
concepts.technical: A bijection between node sets that preserves edges (and here, operator labels). Deciding whether one graph contains another is NP-complete in general (not stated in the book).
concepts.significance: The formal core of program-centric analogy: programs as graphs of operators share exactly matching subgraphs.
concepts.example: The 'loop, skip None, accumulate sum and count, divide' subgraph shared by the two snippets of Figure 19.13.
concepts.misconception: That it measures how similar two graphs are. It is a yes/no exact match on structure.

deeper.title: Similar-looking vs. structurally identical
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, two thought experiments separate the poles:

- **Similar but not structurally identical:** `total / count` and `total // count` look almost the same (one character apart) but compute different things for integers. A distance on the text would call them close. Structurally they are different operators.
- **Structurally identical but not similar-looking:** a loop summing `n` into `ls_sum` and a loop summing `e` into `total` have different names everywhere, yet the operator graph is identical. A naive text similarity might score them low. Program-centric analogy matches them exactly.

This is why the book insists you are 'not trying to compare your classes and functions by *how similar* they look.'

deeper.title: Everyday program-centric analogies
deeper.body:
Examples (not from the book) of 'objects connected by a discrete network of relationships':

1. Realizing that a recipe and an assembly manual share a structure: ordered steps, each with preconditions.
2. Seeing that a new puzzle is a disguised version of one you solved: same constraints, different objects.
3. Recognizing that a legal argument follows the same chain of inferences as a precedent.

In each case the match is about *which elements relate to which, and how*, not about surface resemblance.

misconceptions.claim: Program-centric analogy is just a stricter similarity threshold.
misconceptions.correction: It is a different relation: exact structural identity of parts (subgraph isomorphism), not graded closeness under a distance function.

misconceptions.claim: Only computer scientists and mathematicians use program-centric analogies.
misconceptions.correction: The book says everyone uses them constantly; they underlie reasoning, planning and rigor.

misconceptions.claim: Two code snippets must look alike to share an abstraction.
misconceptions.correction: They can have different names and context; what matters is that some part has exactly the same operator structure.

takeaways: Figure 19.12: instances, similarity clustering, abstract prototypes, the value-centric pipeline.
Tasks you do 'without thinking' rely on value-centric analogies: pattern recognition, perception, intuition.
Program-centric analogy is slower, exact and deliberate: it relates things by exactly shared structure.
Refactoring code into a shared function or base class is program-centric analogy, formally a subgraph isomorphism on graphs of operators.
Program-centric analogies underlie reasoning, planning and rigor, wherever objects are linked by discrete relationships.

questions.question: Which description fits program-centric analogy?
questions.explanation: The book calls it 'slower, exact, deliberate'. 'Immediate, approximate, intuitive' describes value-centric analogy; the other two combinations are not in the book.

questions.question: What formal problem does the book say you solve when looking for shared structure across programs?
questions.answer: Subgraph isomorphism: finding subgraphs of the programs' operator graphs that are exactly shared.
questions.explanation: Programs can be represented as graphs of operators, and shared program subsets are exactly matching subgraphs.

questions.question: Why does the book contrast comparing functions with comparing two human faces?
questions.answer: Faces are compared by how similar they look, through an implicit continuous distance (value-centric). Functions are related by whether parts have exactly the same structure (program-centric). The contrast shows the two kinds of comparison.
questions.explanation: The book says 'You're not trying to compare your classes and functions by how similar they look ... Rather, you're interested in whether there are parts of them that have exactly the same structure.'

questions.question: Subconsciously categorizing movie characters into 'types' is an example of what?
questions.explanation: The book gives this as an example of value-centric abstraction: automatic categorization by similarity, done without thinking.

questions.question: Give a non-programming example of a program-centric analogy and explain why it qualifies.
questions.answer: E.g., realizing that a new scheduling problem has the same constraint structure as one solved before. It qualifies because the relation is about a discrete network of relationships matching exactly, not about surface similarity.
questions.explanation: The book says any time you think about objects connected by a discrete network of relationships, you're using program-centric analogies.

questions.question: Recall the last time you refactored duplicated code. Can you name the shared subgraph you extracted and what became parameters?
questions.answer: Personal answer: the shared structure became the function body; whatever differed (inputs, names) became parameters.
questions.explanation: This is the book's software-engineering example of program-centric analogy, applied to your own experience.
